title: JESUS RAISED A DEAD MAN—AND THE RELIGIOUS LEADERS DECIDED HE HAD TO DIE
paragraphs: JESUS RAISED A DEAD MAN—AND THE RELIGIOUS LEADERS DECIDED HE HAD TO DIE

Lazarus walked out of his grave. Some people believed. Others ran to report Jesus. And before the dust of Bethany had settled, the miracle that proved Jesus gives life became part of the reason powerful men resolved to take His.
There are moments in Scripture so disturbing that you have to read them twice.
Not because they are difficult to understand.
Because they are terrifyingly easy to understand.
A dead man had just walked out of a tomb.
Lazarus had been dead four days.
His sisters had grieved him. Mourners had gathered. The stone had been placed over the entrance. Martha had even warned Jesus about what opening a four-day-old tomb would mean.
This was not someone fainting and recovering.
This was a funeral already underway.
Then Jesus stood outside that grave and cried:
“Lazarus, come forth.”
And the dead man came out.
Imagine being there.
Imagine hearing Mary crying one moment and someone screaming the next.
Imagine staring at a tomb you had watched swallow a man—and then watching that same man emerge wrapped in burial cloths.
Imagine seeing Jesus standing there.
No panic.
No incantation.
No desperate attempt to persuade God.
He called.
Death surrendered.
And then comes one of the darkest twists in the Gospel of John.
You would expect everyone who witnessed or heard about such a sign to fall on their knees.
Some did believe.
But others went to the Pharisees and reported what Jesus had done.
Then the chief priests and Pharisees assembled the council.
Listen carefully to their question.
They did not say, “This man has done nothing.”
They said, in essence:
“What are we doing? This man performs many signs.”
Then came the fear.
If Jesus continued, they reasoned, everyone might believe in Him, and Rome could come and take away their place and their nation.
Think about that.
A man had been raised from the dead...
and they were discussing damage control.
Life had walked out of a grave...
and they were worried about losing control.
That is what makes John 11 so frighteningly personal.
Because sometimes the greatest obstacle between a human heart and Jesus is not lack of evidence.
Sometimes it is the terrifying realization that if Jesus really is who He says He is...
something in us has to surrender.
Our throne.
Our secret sin.
Our reputation.
Our plans.
Our control.
Our comfortable version of Christianity.
Our ability to call ourselves His followers while continuing to live as though we belong to ourselves.
The Greek text of John 11:47 records their admission:
“οὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος πολλὰ ποιεῖ σημεῖα”
houtos ho anthrōpos polla poiei sēmeia
“This man is doing many signs.”
They saw the signs.
Their crisis was what those signs meant.
Because if Jesus truly possessed authority even over death, He could no longer be safely filed away as another teacher.
He demanded a verdict.
And He still does.
Maybe that is why this story feels uncomfortable when we stop treating the Pharisees as distant villains and allow Scripture to search us.
Because there is a little tomb we protect too.
Something behind the stone.
Something we do not want Jesus touching.
Maybe nobody knows about it.
Maybe you sing worship songs while carrying it.
Maybe you quote Scripture while hiding it.
Maybe you have learned how to smile in church, post Christian encouragement online, tell everybody “God is good,” and then return to something privately that is slowly destroying you.
Maybe it is lust.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Pornography.
An affair.
Greed.
Unforgiveness.
Religious hypocrisy.
An addiction.
Secret resentment toward God.
Or maybe it is simply control.
You want Jesus as Savior...
but the thought of Jesus actually becoming Lord over everything terrifies you.
And somewhere inside your soul is the same question echoing from John 11:
What happens to my life if I let Him continue?
Because Jesus does not merely decorate old lives.
He raises dead ones.
Jesus told Martha:
“ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή.”
Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē.
“I am the resurrection and the life.”
Notice what He did not say.
He did not merely say, “I can perform resurrection.”
He said:
“I AM the resurrection.”
Resurrection is not merely something Jesus gives.
Resurrection is bound up in who Jesus is.
That means Martha's deepest hope was standing in front of her while she was still grieving what was lying behind the stone.
Maybe somebody reading this needs that sentence.
Your deepest hope may be closer than your grief has allowed you to see.
Martha looked at a tomb.
Jesus knew a resurrection was coming.
Mary saw four days of death.
Jesus saw something that would display the glory of God.
The mourners saw an ending.
Jesus stood in front of the ending and called it temporary.
And yet...
Jesus wept.
“ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς.”
Edakrysen ho Iēsous.
“Jesus wept.”
Two words in many English translations.
An ocean inside them.
The One who knew Lazarus was about to walk out still wept beside those who were hurting.
That destroys the cruel idea that faith means pain should not hurt.
Jesus knew resurrection was minutes away...
and He still entered their grief.
So when you cry, you are not necessarily demonstrating unbelief.
When your heart breaks, Jesus does not stand far away embarrassed by your weakness.
The Christ who commands graves also weeps beside mourners.
Power and compassion meet in Him.
Then Jesus approached the tomb.
“Take away the stone.”
Martha protested.
Four days.
Too late.
Too much decay.
Too much reality.
Too far gone.
We still speak Martha's language.
“Jesus, You don't understand how long this has been happening.”
“Jesus, You don't know what I've done.”
“Jesus, my marriage is too damaged.”
“Jesus, my child has wandered too far.”
“Jesus, I have failed too many times.”
“Jesus, I promised I would stop and went back again.”
“Jesus, there is already a smell coming from this part of my life.”
And Jesus has never needed your situation to smell alive before He can demonstrate His authority.
Then He cried with a loud voice:
“Λάζαρε, δεῦρο ἔξω.”
Lazare, deuro exō.
“Lazarus, come out.”
And Lazarus came out.
But understand something important.

The raising of Lazarus was an astonishing sign, but Lazarus was restored to mortal life. The New Testament's ultimate resurrection hope is greater still: Jesus Himself would rise never to be conquered by death again, and those who belong to Him are promised resurrection life in Him.
Lazarus therefore points beyond Lazarus.
The tomb at Bethany whispers toward another tomb.
Another stone.
Another morning.
But before Easter morning came...
the cross had to come.
And this is where John 11 becomes breathtaking.
After Lazarus was raised, Caiaphas, the high priest, spoke words whose meaning reached far beyond what he himself intended:
“συμφέρει ὑμῖν ἵνα εἷς ἄνθρωπος ἀποθάνῃ ὑπὲρ τοῦ λαοῦ”
sympherei hymin hina heis anthrōpos apothanē hyper tou laou
“It is better for you that one man should die for the people.”
Caiaphas was thinking politically.
John tells us God was revealing something infinitely greater.
Jesus would die for the nation—and not for that nation only, but to gather God's scattered children into one.
Caiaphas thought Jesus should die to preserve their world.
God would use the death of Jesus to save sinners.
Caiaphas was calculating expediency.
He was unknowingly announcing substitution.
One Man...
dying for the people.
And John 11:53 delivers the chilling consequence:
“ἀπ᾽ ἐκείνης οὖν τῆς ἡμέρας ἐβουλεύσαντο ἵνα ἀποκτείνωσιν αὐτόν.”
Ap' ekeinēs oun tēs hēmeras ebouleusanto hina apokteinōsin auton.
“So from that day they resolved/planned to kill Him.”
Do not miss the terrible irony.
Jesus gave Lazarus his life back...
and powerful men responded by resolving to take Jesus' life.
The One who called a man out of death was now moving toward His own death.
But nobody was ultimately taking Jesus somewhere He was unwilling to go.
Later Jesus would make this unmistakable:
“No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of Myself.”
The cross was not Jesus losing control of His mission.
The cross was His mission.
He knew where the road was going.
He knew betrayal was coming.
He knew the scourge.
The mockery.
The nails.
The darkness.
The abandonment.
The grave.
And He kept walking.
Why?
Because Lazarus was not the only dead man Jesus came to rescue.
We were dead in trespasses and sins.
Not physically buried in Bethany.
Spiritually separated from the God who made us.
And no amount of religious cosmetics could resurrect us.
We did not need self-improvement.
We needed life.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed Someone righteous enough to stand where guilty sinners belonged.
And Jesus Christ went to the cross.
The sinless One for sinners.
The righteous for the unrighteous.
The Shepherd for His sheep.
The Lamb of God bearing sin.
The King wearing thorns.
The Creator pierced by His creatures.
The One who called Lazarus from a grave entered a grave Himself.
And then...
on the third day...
the grave discovered something Lazarus's tomb had already learned:
Death cannot hold the Author of Life.
Jesus rose.
Not metaphorically.
Not merely as an inspirational memory living in His followers.
The proclamation at the center of Christianity is that the crucified Jesus bodily rose from the dead.
And because He lives, repentance is not the funeral of your hope.
It can become the doorway into a new life.
Maybe you have spent years thinking Christianity means cleaning yourself enough that Jesus might finally accept you.
It doesn't.
The Gospel is far more scandalous.
You bring Him your guilt.
He gives grace.
You bring rebellion.
He offers reconciliation.
You bring your record.
He offers His righteousness.
You bring your death.
He gives life.
That does not make sin small.
The cross proves sin is more serious than we wanted to believe.
Grace is not God pretending your rebellion never mattered.
Grace is God providing in Christ what you could never provide for yourself.
That is why repentance matters.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back.
You cannot.
It is turning from sin and turning toward the Savior who paid what you could not pay.
Maybe your scandal is real.
Maybe people know.
Maybe they do not.
Maybe you ruined something precious.
Maybe you betrayed somebody.
Maybe you abandoned God after promising you never would.
Maybe your Christianity became performance.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying something you desperately hope nobody discovers.
Hear this carefully:
Jesus did not come merely for people whose stories already look respectable.
He came to save sinners.
That does not excuse what happened.
It means what happened does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted His church.
The dying criminal beside Jesus had nothing left to repair his reputation with.
Yet throughout Scripture, grace keeps appearing where human beings expect only endings.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by eliminating repentance.
He rewrites everything by meeting guilty people with truth, mercy, forgiveness, and transforming grace purchased through His own blood.
The Gospel does not merely give your old life better publicity.
Christ gives new life.
And perhaps the most dangerous thing you can do after reading about Lazarus is admire the miracle while refusing the Man.
The religious leaders were close enough to hear extraordinary testimony about what Jesus had done.
Yet proximity to the evidence did not automatically produce surrender.
So this article eventually has to stop being about Caiaphas.
It has to stop being about Lazarus.
It has to stop being about Martha.
It has to become about you.
What will you do with Jesus?
Not Christianity as culture.
Not church attendance.
Not religious Facebook posts.
Jesus.
The One who says:
“I am the resurrection and the life.”
If He is who He claimed to be, neutrality is an illusion.
And if something inside you has been whispering while you read this...
“Come out.”
Come out of hiding.
Come out of secret compromise.
Come out of pretending.
Come out of the exhausting performance of trying to look alive while dying inside.
Bring the sin into His light.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Call upon Christ.
You do not have to make yourself alive before coming to the One who raises the dead.
Come to Jesus.
And if you have wandered from Him, return.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one more secret night.
Not after you somehow become worthy.
Come broken.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
But come.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need to know that Jesus still restores broken lives.

Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not. We are saved by grace through faith, not by social-media activity—but because glorifying God includes making His truth known. If Christ has given us good news, love should make us want somebody else to hear it.
Someone whose marriage feels dead.
Someone secretly returning to addiction.
Someone angry with God.
Someone contemplating giving up on faith.
Send it privately to the friend who has gone quiet.
It never could.
Not because supporting a ministry makes you more righteous before God.
Only Christ saves.
This is not merely about consuming more Christian content.
The goal is Christ.
To know Him.
To know His Word.
To repent more deeply.
To recognize deception more quickly.
To love truth more fiercely.
To become more faithful when nobody is watching.
To carry the Gospel farther than we could carry it alone.
Because somewhere tonight there is another Martha staring at something she believes is beyond repair.
Another Mary crying where nobody can see.
Another Lazarus-shaped situation everyone has already declared finished.
Another believer hiding behind grave clothes Jesus never intended them to keep wearing.
And another soul who needs to hear that Christianity is not ultimately the story of human beings climbing their way toward God.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue sinners.
The story of the Holy One touching the unclean.
The Innocent standing in the place of the guilty.
The rejected King wearing a crown of thorns.
The crucified Savior entering death.
The risen Christ walking out victorious.
The resurrection and the life calling dead hearts home.
Bethany began with sickness.
Then grief.
Then a tomb.
Then tears.
Then a voice.
Then a dead man walked out.
And the miracle became one more step on the road toward Calvary, where Jesus would accomplish something infinitely greater than postponing one man's physical death.
He would give Himself for sinners.
So when your story reaches the page you wish you could tear out...
when shame tells you the ending has already been written...
when Satan points toward the tomb and whispers, “Look what you became”...
remember the Man standing outside Lazarus's grave.
Remember the Savior walking deliberately toward His cross.
Remember the stone rolled away on resurrection morning.
Remember that Jesus Christ is still Lord when your story looks impossible.
And remember this:
The grave may contain a chapter of your story, but when your life belongs to the risen Christ, the grave does not get to write the final sentence.
